note: Jared Goff has been strong for fantasy through two games as the QB7 in fantasy points per game. Among 28 qualifying passers, he has been sixth-best in passer rating and passing success rate, 11th in highly accurate throw rate, and tenth in hero throw rate. Goff will have to contend with the Lions' former defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn this week, who has the Jets' pass defense off to a fast start. Now, I do also have to mention that the Jets have faced Cam Ward and Jordan Love so far, so take it with a grain of salt. Ward and Love have begun the season with struggle bus games. The Jets have allowed the ninth-lowest passing success rate, the sixth-lowest EPA per dropback, and the third-lowest explosive pass rate. Those are impressive stats. The Jets are also fifth in pressure rate and eighth in blitz rate. Goff has destroyed the blitz so far this season, ranking seventh in passing success rate and second in passer rating. I think Goff will still have success this week despite the Jets' defensive quick start out of the blocks.

Trevor Lawrence has been Jekyll and Hyde to begin the season. He beat up on the Browns as the QB5 for the week, and then he was the QB26 in weekly scoring last week against Denver. Among 28 qualifying quarterbacks, he ranks seventh in yards per attempt, fifth in passing success rate, 20th in highly accurate throw rate, 25th in hero throw rate, and he has the highest turnover-worthy play rate. There's a lot of good there while also plenty of concerning data points. He has another tough matchup against the Pats this week. Yes, New England has only faced Drew Lock and Aaron Rodgers this season, so take their metrics with a grain of salt. They have also held those passers to the second-lowest EPA per dropback, the 14th-lowest passing success rate, and the tenth-lowest explosive pass rate. If you're being an optimist, this is a neutral matchup being propped up metrically by facing subpar passers. With Lawrence's concerning metrics, I'm a little more worried about him than that viewpoint would suggest.

Tyler Shough is the QB5 in fantasy points per game. No, that's not a typo. He has been awesome for fantasy. Shough is also playing good football from a "real" football perspective. Among 29 qualifying passers, he is 15th in yards per attempt and passing success rate, 16th in highly accurate throw rate, 14th in catchable target rate, and FIRST in hero throw rate. Shough has started slowly in both games before turning it on in the second halves. The Raiders (on paper) look like a tougher matchup for Shough, but they have only faced Justin Herbert and Malik Willis, so I'm willing to take the Raiders' defensive stats with a grain of salt. Las Vegas has held passers to the eighth-lowest passing success rate, the sixth-lowest EPA per dropback, and the 13th-fewest fantasy points per dropback. The one area that I do think is real for the Raiders is the fact that they are eighth-best in pressure rate. Luckily for Shough, he has the third-best yards per attempt and fourth-best passing success rate against pressure through two games. I think this is another strong game for Shough.

Jordan Love hasn't played well to begin the season. Yes, he's the QB13 in fantasy points per game, but that's on the strength of a high-passing-volume Week 1, which carried him to QB11 for that week. Last week, he fell to QB20 in weekly scoring. Love has been struggling as a passer. Among 29 qualifying passers, Love does have the 12th-highest yards per attempt and the ninth-highest aDOT, but he also has the fourth-lowest passing success rate, the lowest highly accurate throw rate and catchable target rate, and the highest off-target rate. Love could struggle again this week against a pass defense that has the third-best pressure rate while allowing the third-lowest passing success rate, the 11th-fewest yards per attempt, and the 14th-fewest EPA per dropback.

Drake Maye has struggled out of the gate as the QB28 in fantasy. Among 28 qualifying passers, he is 17th in yards per attempt, 21st in passing success rate, has the 12th-lowest aDOT, the second-highest turnover-worthy play rate, and the tenth-lowest EPA per dropback. It has been rough. His rushing hasn't been enough to save his fantasy days, averaging 5.5 rushing attempts and 32 yards on the ground. This week's matchup against the Jags should be seen at worst as a neutral one with the upside to be quite favorable. Jacksonville's talented defense has also been meh through two games. The Jaguars have allowed the 14th-highest passing success rate, the highest explosive pass rate, and they rank 14th-best in EPA per dropback allowed. I'm not expecting a HUGE bounce-back game from Maye, but I also won't be shocked if he logs his first QB1 outing of the season in Week 3.

Justin Herbert and the Chargers offense have been utterly disappointing through two weeks. Herbert is the QB26 in fantasy points per game. Among 28 qualifying passers, Herbert ranks 12th in yards per attempt and 14th in highly accurate throw rate, but he also has the seventh-lowest passing success rate, the seventh-highest turnover-worthy throw rate, and the eighth-lowest fantasy points per dropback. Maybe Herbert turns things around this week against a struggling Bills pass defense, but he has faceplanted the last two weeks against lesser defenses. I'm not holding my breath that we see him looking like an MVP candidate in Week 3, but it's possible. The Bills have allowed the tenth-most yards per attempt, the fourth-highest passing success rate, and the sixth-most EPA per dropback.

Kyler Murray has cleared the concussion protocol and will start in Week 3. In Week 1, Murray played only 11 snaps before leaving the game. He completed three of his five passes with 3.6 yards per attempt. This is essentially Murray's first start of the season. Murray could have success this week if he can withstand the blitz. Tampa Bay has blitzed at the fifth-highest rate in the NFL (44.4%). Since 2024, among 25 qualifying quarterbacks, Murray ranks 24th in yards per attempt and dead last in EPA per dropback against the blitz. If Murray can reverse this trend, he should have a nice day against a pass defense that has allowed the 14th-most yards per attempt, the ninth-highest passing success rate, and the 14th-highest EPA per dropback. The Bucs also have the seventh-lowest pressure rate, so the blitzes haven't been getting home. I have cautious hope for Murray this week.

After two games, Bryce Young is the QB2 in fantasy points per game. Yes, it's insane, but it's true. I think Young can keep the train rolling this week, but I'm worried about his ability to do this for the entire season. Among 29 qualifying passers, Young ranks third in yards per attempt, tenth in passing success rate, and eighth in hero throw rate, BUT he also has the second-lowest catchable target rate, the second-lowest highly accurate throw rate, and has faced the ninth-lowest pressure rate. There's a ton of volatility in that statistical profile when you also realize he is second in deep ball rate. Big risk. Big reward, but the other side of the coin could eventually show itself. I think Young can keep up the magic act this week, though. The Browns have allowed the fifth-highest passing success rate, the seventh-highest passer rating, the fifth-highest CPOE, and logged the 11th-lowest pressure rate. Young should have time to pick apart this pass defense in Week 3.

Bo Nix has had a rough start to the season as the QB30 in fantasy points per game. Nix did show signs of life last week after a wretched game in Week 1. Last week, among 32 qualifying passers, Nix ranked fourth in yards per attempt, 10th in passing success rate, 11th in aDOT, seventh in highly accurate throw rate, and 12th in catchable target rate. We'll see if Nix can keep the good times rolling this week or if he'll turn back into a pumpkin. The Rams have allowed the third-fewest yards per attempt, the tenth-lowest passing success rate, and the fifth-fewest EPA per dropback.

Matthew Stafford looked exactly like the guy we thought we were getting in Week 1 last week. He ripped the Giants' secondary apart as the QB6 for the week. Stafford had 327 passing yards and four scores. He amassed 10.5 yards per attempt with a 74.2% highly accurate throw rate, a 6.5% hero throw rate, and a 93.5% catchable target rate. You can't get much better than that. This week, he'll face a Denver pass defense that has held passers to the tenth-fewest yards per attempt, the 13th-lowest passing success rate, and the 12th-fewest EPA per dropback. We'll see if he can keep the train rolling. I wouldn't be surprised if Stafford posts another strong QB1 performance or if he looks closer to the quarterback we saw in Week 1. There's a wide range of outcomes here for Stafford in Week 3.

Through two games, the fantasy success hasn't been there for Geno Smith (QB23), but that could change this week. Smith has operated as a solid game manager for his first two outings with the Jets. Among 28 qualifying passers, Smith has ranked 15th in yards per attempt, 16th in passing success rate, and sixth in catchable target rate, but he has also had the eighth-lowest aDOT and the tenth-lowest hero throw rate. Smith has been asked to operate quickly as a point guard. That could work well in Week 3. The Lions' pass defense has been a hollow shell through two games, allowing the eighth-highest passing success rate and the 11th-most EPA per dropback. They have also ranked second-best in blitz rate and pressure rate. Their ability to get home with the pass rush will be huge, but Smith has been strong against the blitz as a Jet, ranking fourth-best in yards per attempt and fifth in passing success rate. Smith is a strong QB2 this week who could surprise with fringe QB1 production.

C.J. Stroud is the QB15 in fantasy points per game. He still (per the metrics) resembles the struggling passer that we have seen for the last few seasons. Among 29 qualifying passers, Stroud has the seventh-fewest yards per attempt, the 11th-lowest passing success rate, the sixth-highest off-target rate, and the fifth-lowest catchable target rate. There's nothing good to take away from that collection of stats. Stroud can continue to be awful this week and still walk away with a solid QB2 week against Indy's porous pass defense. Indy has allowed the highest yards per attempt, the fourth-highest passing success rate, the fourth-most EPA per dropback, and the fourth-highest CPOE.

I'll admit it. I didn't see Baker Mayfield laying a goose egg against Cleveland, but it happened. Call me crazy, but his numbers suggest better days are ahead. Among 29 qualifying passers, he is 11th in passing success rate, 14th in highly accurate throw rate, and 12th in catchable target rate. Mayfield has had to suffer from the seventh-highest drop rate and the second-most passing yards lost to drops (57). Mayfield will HAVE TO navigate the blitz to have success this week. Brian Flores has directed a pass defense that has blitzed on 73.9% of their defense snaps, which is the highest rate in the NFL. Minnesota has generated the fourth-highest pressure rate. The Vikings have allowed the ninth-highest explosive pass rate. Minnesota has also allowed the third-lowest passing success rate and the 13th-fewest EPA per dropback. When opposing passing attacks have connected, it has been for big plays. It just doesn't happen often. Since 2024, among 40 quarterbacks against the blitz, Mayfield ranks 11th in passer rating and passing success rate and 13th in fantasy points per dropback. Go back to the Mayfield well again this week if you need (risky) upside.

Through two games, Malik Willis has finished as the QB13 and the QB22 in weekly fantasy scoring. The big difference from Week 1 to Week 2 was the decline in his rushing output. In Week 1, Willis had six rushing attempts with 39 yards on the ground and a score. Last week, he ran only twice for six yards. That's not nearly enough rushing production to support him in fantasy. I hope that was an outlier and not the beginning of a worrisome trend. If that continues, Willis's fantasy value for 2026 will be capsized. His overall accuracy has been worrisome, but the flashes of arm talent have been there. Among 28 qualifying passers, Willis ranks eighth in yards per attempt and second in hero throw rate, but he also has the third-lowest passing success rate, the fifth-lowest highly accurate throw rate, and the eighth-lowest catchable target rate. It's also notable that he has dealt with the tenth-highest drop rate from his receivers. Sit Willis this week. Spags will have him in a blender. The Chiefs have allowed the fourth-fewest yards per attempt, the third-lowest EPA per dropback, and the third-fewest fantasy points per dropback.

Jacoby Brissett is the QB27 in fantasy points per game as he's playing point guard, aka dink and dunk quarterback. Among 29 qualifying passers, he ranks 19th in highly accurate throw rate and 16th in catchable target rate despite the third-fewest yards per attempt, the sixth-lowest aDOT, and the third-lowest hero throw rate. Brissett is headed for another long day against a pass defense that has allowed the third-lowest passing success rate, the second-lowest CPOE, and the fifth-fewest fantasy points per dropback.

Through two games of the 2026 NFL season, Kirk Cousins is the QB11 in fantasy points per game. Do I expect this to continue all season? Nope. Do I also need to show Kirko Chainz some respect? Yep. Among 29 qualifying passers, he has been average on a per-dropback basis, ranking 19th in yards per attempt, 21st in passing success rate (13th-highest aDOT), 20th in highly accurate throw rate, and fourth-best in catchable target rate. Cousins has been better than many expected to begin the season. I don't know if Cousins has another standout performance in him for Week 3, but he's a viable streaming option and should return at least strong QB2 production this week. The Saints rank 17th in EPA per dropback allowed while giving up the sixth-highest passing success rate and 11th-highest CPOE.

In his two starts this season, Deshaun Watson has finished as the QB21 and QB12 in weekly fantasy scoring. Watson has been a low aDOT point guard for the offense. Among 29 qualifying passers, he has the third-lowest aDOT, the fourth-highest rate of passing yards that have been from YAC (59.6%), the 11th-highest off-target rate, and the seventh-highest turnover-worthy throw rate. Watson will likely have a Week 3 performance closer to Week 1 against the Panthers' pass defense that has allowed the 11th-fewest yards per attempt, the tenth-lowest passing success rate, and the tenth-lowest EPA per dropback.

Daniel Jones has looked like 2025 Kirk Cousins through two starts as the QB28 in fantasy points per game. The arm velocity has been meh, and he's been a low aDOT point guard. Among 29 qualifying passers, he has the fourth-fewest yards per attempt, the 14th-lowest passing success rate, the second-lowest aDOT (5.98), and the ninth-highest off-target throw rate. Houston's pass defense has been dreadful after two games, but I still can't believe in Jones as anything more than a snooze-worthy QB2 this week. Houston has allowed the third-most yards per attempt, the 14th-highest passing success rate, and the seventh-most EPA per dropback.

With Jaxson Dart out for the rest of the season, it looks like Jameis Winston will be New York's starting quarterback. If last week is any indication of what we can expect from Winston at this stage of his career, it might be a dumpster fire. Winston had a 40.7% completion rate, 4.1 yards per attempt, a 63% catchable target rate, and a 33.3% off-target rate. I don't care who Winston is playing at this point. I need to see at least one game of better football from him before I'm willing to plug him into any lineup in any format.

It has been a rough start to the 2026 season for Aaron Rodgers as the QB30 in fantasy points per game. He has failed to eclipse 13 fantasy points in either game. There's no metric that I can unearth that can convince you to start him in fantasy at this point. Among 28 qualifying passers, he has the second-fewest yards per attempt, the second-lowest passing success rate, the 13th-lowest aDOT, the eighth-lowest highly accurate throw rate, and the ninth-lowest hero throw rate. He doesn't run at this stage of his career. There's nothing good here. Don't play Rodgers in any format this week.

Michael Penix will make his 2026 season debut this week, coming off a torn ACL. Last year, he was the QB26 in fantasy points per game with only three QB1 outings in weekly scoring. Among 43 qualifying passers, he was 17th in yards per attempt, 21st in passing success rate, and 42nd in highly accurate throw rate and catchable target rate. There's not a ton to love there. Penix could have a rough start to his season against a pass defense that has allowed the sixth-fewest yards per attempt, the ninth-lowest passing success rate, the 14th-fewest fantasy points per dropback, and has generated the tenth-best pressure rate.

Marcus Mariota will draw the start for Washington this week after Jayden Daniels' injury last week. Mariota could be their starting quarterback for the rest of the season. Last year, in his seven full games started, Mariota finished as a QB1 three times (QB6, QB9, QB3). In those seven games, Mariota averaged 6.4 rushing attempts and 36.7 rushing yards. He added only one rushing score from those games. Last season, among 38 qualifying passers, Mariota ranked 11th in yards per attempt, 26th in passing success rate, 27th in highly accurate throw rate, and sixth in hero throw rate. I don't expect a big day for Mariota in Week 3 against arguably the best pass defense in the NFL. Seattle has allowed the eighth-fewest EPA per dropback, the seventh-lowest passing success rate, and the second-lowest explosive passing rate. Mariota is a low-end QB2 for Week 3.

Cam Ward is the QB20 in fantasy points per game. Ward has been dreadful as a passer through two games. Among 29 qualifying passers, Ward has the fifth-fewest yards per attempt, the third-lowest highly accurate throw rate, the fourth-lowest catchable target rate, and the 12th-highest off-target rate. The Giants have been equally bad as a pass defense. We have an old fashioned "mid off" this week with Ward against the Giants' pass defense. We'll see who wins, but Ward could return decent QB2 production this week. New York has allowed the 12th-most yards per attempt, the eighth-highest passing success rate, the second-most EPA per dropback, and the fourth-most fantasy points per dropback.

Caleb Williams hasn't practiced this week (hamstring). Tyson Bagent has also not practiced this week (concussion). I'm expecting Case Keenum to be under center for Chicago in Week 3. The last time we saw Keenum starting in the NFL was in 2023. Keenum made two starts for the Texans in that season. He only played the entire game in one of those weeks, finishing as the QB24 for fantasy. Keenum completed 63.9% of his passes (229 passing yards with one score and one pick). He had only 6.4 yards per attempt. The Eagles have limited passers to the ninth-fewest yards per attempt and the lowest passing success rate. Expecting Keenum to produce more than middling QB2 numbers is probably asking too much from him this week.

Sam Darnold will be back under center for Seattle this week. He had full practices on Thursday and Friday of this week (glute). Darnold left Week 1's action after only two passing attempts, so there's nothing to take away from that game with Darnold. Last year, Darnold was awesome on a per-dropback basis, ranking second in yards per attempt, seventh in passing success rate, first in highly accurate throw rate, and fourth in hero throw rate. In Seattle's run-first offense, Darnold had only seven weekly finishes as a QB1 in fantasy while finishing as the QB24 or lower in weekly scoring eight times. This feels like a great spot to let him air it out some. Washington has allowed the fifth-most yards per attempt, the 12th-highest passing success rate, the highest passer rating, and the fourth-most EPA per dropback. Darnold could flirt with QB1 production this week.

Drew Lock hasn't been much of a fantasy factor over the last two weeks, finishing as the QB23 in weekly scoring in both weeks. Lock has played much better than those fantasy finishes imply. Among 28 qualifying quarterbacks, Lock has ranked fifth in yards per attempt, seventh in passing success rate, seventh in highly accurate throw rate, and 12th in hero throw rate. I don't expect Lock to have a monster fantasy day in Week 3, but he should have another efficient outing against a struggling Commanders' pass defense. Washington has allowed the fifth-most yards per attempt, the 12th-highest passing success rate, the highest passer rating, and the fourth-most EPA per dropback. Sam Darnold has returned to practice, but we have to see him ramp up his practice schedule before I'm willing to project him to start in Week 3. For now, I still think it'll be Lock under center in Week 3.

Do I think Caleb Williams will play this week after last week's hamstring injury? No, but Chicago hasn't ruled out him playing this week. Tyson Bagent is also in concussion protocol. I think we'll eventually see Case Keenum named Chicago's starting quarterback for Week 3, but for now I'll wait and see what practice reports look like and update this situation on Saturday.

De'Von Achane is the RB23 in fantasy points per game, averaging 19 touches and 79.5 total yards per game. Through two games, he has been inefficient with his touches despite seeing league-average offensive line play (21st in yards before contact per attempt among 43 qualifying rushers). Among 43 qualifying rushers, Achane ranks 31st in explosive run rate, 38th in yards after contact per attempt, and 35th in missed tackle rate. He has dominated the backfield work for Miami with an 82.9% snap rate, 66% of the rushing attempts, a 73.8% route share, and a 22% target share. Achane could find decent running room this week against a run defense that has allowed the tenth-highest rushing success rate, has the 12th-lowest stuff rate, and has given up the 14th-most yards before contact per attempt.

With Jonathon Brooks on the IR, Chuba Hubbard will retain his workhorse role for Carolina for the foreseeable future and possibly the entire season. Hubbard has averaged 13.5 touches and 75.5 total yards as the RB8 in fantasy points per game. Among 43 qualifying backs, Hubbard ranks 17th in yards after contact per attempt and 15th in missed tackle rate. Hubbard should have another strong outing against a run defense that has allowed the sixth-highest explosive run rate, the fourth-highest rushing success rate, and the tenth-highest missed tackle rate.

Kyren Williams is the RB14 in fantasy points per game, averaging 14 touches and 81 total yards. Williams has a 59% snap rate, 40.4% of the rushing attempts, a 54.8% route share, and an 8.5% target share. Williams has handled six of the eight running back red zone rushing attempts for the Rams. Among 43 qualifying backs, he ranks ninth in explosive run rate and 11th in missed tackle rate. Williams should have another nice outing in Week 3 against a run defense that has allowed the 13th-highest explosive run rate, the most yards after contact per attempt, and the highest missed tackle rate.

Jaylen Warren should be a workhorse for Pittsburgh this week with Rico Dowdle out (toe). Warren is dealing with a shoulder issue, but he had limited practices all week and has been listed as questionable. The only other running back on the Steelers' roster is Eli Heidenreich. I doubt they want to lean on the talented rookie in an expanded role this week, so Warren should get all the work he can handle this week. Warren has been his usual hyper-efficient self this season. Among 43 qualifying rushers, he ranks 14th in yards after contact per attempt and 13th in missed tackle rate while posting 1.65 YPRR through the air. Warren's matchup this week is against an improved Cincy run defense that, at best, is a neutral matchup, but I'm more worried about the matchup. Warren will need volume to overcome it, and he'll likely get the touch count to do so. Cincy has allowed the 13th-lowest explosive run rate while having the second-highest rate of contacting backs at or behind the line of scrimmage. This run defense also sits at 15th in yards after contact per attempt and 16th in missed tackle rate allowed.

Bucky Irving has been awesome so far as the RB11 in fantasy points per game. He has averaged 18 touches and 91.5 total yards. Irving has had a 71.1% snap rate, 55.6 % of the rushing attempts, a 56.6% route share, and a 17.7% target share. The usage has been awesome. Among 43 qualifying rushers, he ranks 16th in explosive run rate and 11th in yards after contact per attempt. Minnesota's run defense is similar to their passing defense. They don't give up a ton of big plays, but when they do, they are explosives. The Vikes have allowed the third-lowest rushing success rate while logging the fourth-highest stuff rate. The other side of the coin is they also have allowed the fifth-highest explosive run rate, the 12th-most yards before contact per attempt, and the tenth-highest yards per carry to gap runs. 48% of Irving's runs have been gap, and he ranks fifth in gap yards per carry (6.92). I think Irving has another solid day in Week 3.

D'Andre Swift is the RB5 in fantasy points per game, averaging 20 touches and 116 total yards per game. Swift has eight of the team's 11 red zone running back carries. Swift has a 61.4% snap rate, 48.6% of the rushing attempts, a 32.5% route share, and a 9.4% target share. Among 43 qualifying backs, Swift ranks sixth in yards after contact per attempt and eighth in missed tackle rate. Swift should have success again this week. Philly has allowed the ninth-highest explosive run rate, the fifth-most yards after contact per attempt, and the fifth-highest missed tackle rate.

Last week, Aaron Jones sustained a knee injury. He finished the game wearing a brace. This week, Jones sat out of practice on Wednesday, was limited on Thursday, and had a full session on Friday. Jones doesn't carry an injury designation into this week's game, but he's clearly not 100%. Last week, he had an 80.4% snap rate, an 82.1% rushing share, a 41.7% route share, and zero targets. He finished with 23 touches and 105 rushing yards. I doubt he gets anywhere close to that type of workload this week. In Week 1, Jones had a 42.6% snap rate, a 35.3% rushing share, and a 23.3% route share (4.2% target share) as he finished with 13 touches and 40 total yards. I'd expect a workload close to Week 1 against the Bucs or somewhere in the middle ground of these two games. The Vikes don't have another healthy back that they trust like Jones. DeeJay Dallas could assist some on early downs while taking on pass-pro snaps to lessen Jones' workload. Jones has acted his age in the efficiency department with only 1.80 yards after contact per attempt and a 9% missed tackle rate. With all of these concerns, Jones is only a middling flex play this week with a bad matchup. Tampa Bay has limited backs to the sixth-lowest explosive run rate, the fifth-lowest rushing success rate, and the seventh-lowest EPA per rush.

Last week, David Montgomery's workload went out the window. He played only 53.2% of the snaps after dominating the snap count for most of Week 1. Montgomery also had only a 33.3% rushing attempt share and 41.9% route share (3.6% target share). He finished with eight touches and 24 total yards. Montgomery also split the red zone rushing role, with both he and Woody Marks getting an attempt inside the 20-yard line last week. Montgomery's rushing metrics have been rough after two games, while the offensive line has given him only 1.15 yards before contact per attempt. Montgomery has a 4.5% explosive run rate, 1.54 yards after contact per attempt, and a 12% missed tackle rate. If Houston can play with a lead, Montgomery could have a bounceback game this week against Indy's putrid run defense. Indy has allowed the third-highest explosive run rate, the sixth-highest rushing success rate, the seventh-most yards before contact per attempt, and the fourth-highest missed tackle rate.

Last week, with Najee Harris active, Cam Skattebo retained the lead-back role with a 60% snap rate, 57.1% of the rushing attempts, and a 55.9% route share (12.5% target share). He did lose out to Harris in the red zone, with Harris seeing two red zone rushing attempts while Skattebo had one. We'll see if that sticks this week. Skattebo is the RB22 in fantasy points per game, averaging 17 touches and 68 total yards. Skattebo has a "decent" 2.0 yards after contact per attempt and a 17% missed tackle rate. If he's going to have a nice Week 3, it'll have to be because of his workload/volume, because the matchup isn't great and I don't know how often Jameis Winston will have the offense in the red zone. Tennessee has allowed the lowest explosive run rate, the 13th-lowest rushing success rate, and the 11th-fewest yards after contact per attempt.

Jeremiyah Love has played behind Tyler Allgeier in both games this season. Does it make a ton of sense? Nope. It's the Cardinals, though. Love has a 42.9% snap rate, a 39.2% rushing attempt share, and a 32.9% route share (10.8% target share). Love has averaged only 12.5 touches and 47.5 total yards as the RB25 in fantasy points per game. In limited duty, Love has posted an outstanding 2.85 yards after contact per attempt with a 15% missed tackle rate. Love is only a flex play this week with a bad matchup. The 49ers have held teams to the fifth-lowest explosive run rate, the seventh-fewest yards after contact per attempt, and the sixth-lowest missed tackle rate.

Quinshon Judkins is the RB33 in fantasy points per game, averaging 15.5 touches and 49 total yards per game. Judkins has a 68.3% snap rate with 53.3% of the rushing attempts, a 38.5% route share, and a 13.5% target share. He has handled all three of the Browns' red zone rushing attempts this season. Unfortunately, he has been woefully inefficient with his workload, with zero explosive runs, 1.42 yards after contact per attempt, and an 8% missed tackle rate. He could easily have his best game of this season this week, though. That's how bad the Carolina run defense is. Carolina has allowed the 11th-highest explosive run rate, the third-highest rushing success rate, and the second-most yards after contact per attempt.

Bhayshul Tuten has seen consistency in his workload through two games, with designed carry shares of 51.7% and 54.2% and route shares of 34.5% and 33.3%. He has averaged 15.5 touches and 75 total yards while splitting the red zone rushing role with Chris Rodriguez (each has two red zone rushing attempts). Tuten has been stellar on a per-rush basis. Among 41 qualifying backs, he ranks sixth in explosive run rate, tenth in rushing success rate, and third-best in missed tackle rate behind only Kenneth Walker and Saquon Barkley. Tuten has a tougher matchup this week. He'll need another touchdown this week to pay off for fantasy. New England has allowed the 14th-lowest explosive run rate, the tenth-lowest rushing success rate, and has ranked 15th in missed tackle rate.

The backfield for New Orleans has been a mess through two games. Last week, with Alvin Kamara back, Travis Etienne led the backfield with a 53.1% snap rate, but he had only 29.6% of the rushing attempts (Kamara 33.3%) and a 33.3% route share (Kamara 23.1%). Kamara had a 17.6% target share while Etienne lagged behind with only a 5.9% share. Etienne finished with ten touches and 31 total yards. This isn't the type of usage that anyone (including myself) projected for Etienne entering this season. Kamara also got the team's only running back red zone rushing attempt. Etienne has posted a respectable 11.8% explosive run rate and 18% missed tackle rate. Etienne could be an RB2 with a bad matchup this week, but he's best viewed as a risky flex at this point until his usage improves. The Raiders have allowed the tenth-lowest explosive run rate, the seventh-lowest rushing success rate, and the fourth-lowest missed tackle rate. Etienne popped up on the injury report this week with a hamstring issue. He had limited practices on Wednesday and Thursday, but he upgraded to a full session on Friday. He doesn't carry an injury designation into this game.

Last week, Rhamondre Stevenson happened to fumble in his first game with his running mate, TreVeyon Henderson, back. The Pats proceeded to penalize Stevenson for his usual fumbling issues and handed the backfield reins to Henderson. Henderson played 60.4% of the snaps with 57.1% of the rushing attempts and a 40.7% route share. Henderson finished with 16 carries and 76 rushing yards (one score, zero targets) as the RB13 for the week. He flashed his usual explosiveness with a long run of 39 yards, accounting for over half of his yards for the day. Outside of that, Henderson's per-touch efficiency was subpar with a 31.3% rushing success rate, 1.19 yards after contact per attempt, and a 13% missed tackle rate. I have no clue if the Pats will immediately hand the steering wheel of the rushing offense back to Stevenson this week as they have in the past or if this creates an opening for Henderson. I'm avoiding starting anyone from the New England backfield this week, but if you're forced to start Henderson, the matchup is at least good. Jacksonville ranks 17th in explosive run rate allowed while also surrendering the 12th-highest rushing success rate, the fifth-most yards before contact per attempt, and has the fifth-lowest rate of contacting the rusher at or behind the line of scrimmage.

Coming off a Week 1 where Rhamondre Stevenson was New England's bell cow, we saw Stevenson quickly get into the doghouse and not come out in Week 2. Stevenson did Stevenson things and fumbled away his lead-back role. As punishment for his butter fingers, Stevenson played only 35.8% of the snaps with 21.4% of the designed carries. He had a 37% route share and a 9.1% target share. Stevenson finished with seven touches and 46 total yards. This backfield looks like a headache again with TreVeyon Henderson back and Stevenson fumbling the bag. New England has gone immediately back to him in the following week after fumbling issues, but there's no way of telling if that will be the case in Week 3. I'm avoiding putting Stevenson in lineups this week if I can help it because of this uncertainty. If you have to go this route, it's at least a good matchup on the ground to help talk yourself into it. Jacksonville ranks 17th in explosive run rate allowed while also surrendering the 12th-highest rushing success rate, the fifth-most yards before contact per attempt, and has the fifth-lowest rate of contacting the rusher at or behind the line of scrimmage.

Tony Pollard missed practice on Wednesday (ankle). Tyjae Spears also sustained an ankle injury last week. Pollard seems to be the healthier of the two. Pollard returned to limited practice sessions on Thursday and Friday. Spears didn't practice until Friday of this week and only logged a limited session. Pollard doesn't carry an injury designation into this week, while Spears is questionable. Pollard has handled five of the team's seven running back red zone rushing attempts this season. Last week, he finished with 15 touches and 65 total yards with a 52.9% snap rate, 48.3% of the rushing attempts, a 37.5% route share, and a 5% target share. On a per-touch basis, Pollard has been awesome through two games. Among 43 qualifying backs, he is tenth in explosive run rate, eighth in yards after contact per attempt, and ninth in missed tackle rate. Pollard could have a strong RB2 week against a porous Giants' run defense that has allowed the fourth-highest explosive run rate, the second-highest rushing success rate, and the ninth-highest missed tackle rate.

Jadarian Price sustained a chest injury last week in the late third quarter. Price returned to limited practices this week on Wednesday and Thursday. He had a full session on Friday and doesn't carry an injury designation into this week's game. Mike Macdonald has stated that Price will be a full-go this week. Last week, in the first half, Price had a 46.7% snap rate, 60% of the rushing attempts, and a 26.7% route share. In those two quarters, Emanuel Wilson had a 40% rushing share while George Holani led the backfield with a 40% route share. It was closer than that appears in the route department, with Price seeing four routes compared to Holani's six. Price has been amazing on a per-touch basis after two games. Among 43 qualifying backs, he ranks sixth in explosive run rate, fifth in yards after contact per attempt, and sixth in missed tackle rate. If Seattle really unleashes Price this week, I think he can have a surprising week. Washington has held backs to the 11th-lowest rushing success rate, but they have also allowed the seventh-highest missed tackle rate and have the 12th-lowest rate of hitting backs at or behind the line of scrimmage. They have also been gashed by zone runs, giving up the tenth-most zone yards per carry (4.6) while ranking 15th in zone rushing success rate allowed (Price, 87% zone). Last season, Washington allowed the fifth-highest rushing success rate, the tenth-highest explosive run rate, and the ninth-most EPA per rush to zone runs.

Blake Corum's value is entirely based upon his rushing stats. He doesn't have a red zone carry through two games, but I expect that he'll start to work into that area of the field for the Rams eventually. Corum has averaged 11.5 touches and 73 total yards. Among 43 qualifying backs, he is second in explosive run rate and third-best in missed tackle rate. Corum is a strong flex play this week with a wonderful matchup. The Broncos have allowed the 13th-highest explosive run rate, the most yards after contact per attempt, and the highest missed tackle rate.

Kyle Monangai is the RB17 in fantasy points per game thanks to his big Week 1 game. Monangai has averaged 12 touches and 91 total yards with three of the backfield's 11 red zone rushing attempts. Among 43 qualifying backs, Monangai ranks fourth in explosive run rate and first in yards after contact per attempt. He has had a 39.3% snap rate, 28.6% of the rushing attempts, and a 26.3% route share (6.3% target share). Monangai is a solid flex play this week. Philly has allowed the ninth-highest explosive run rate, the fifth-most yards after contact per attempt, and the fifth-highest missed tackle rate.

Last week, Woody Marks had a larger share of the Houston backfield with a 45.5% snap share, a 44.4% rushing attempt share, and a 37.1% route share (10.7% target share). Marks split the red zone rushing role with David Montgomery, with each getting a tote inside the 20-yard line. Last week, he finished with 13 touches and 35 total yards. So far this season, Marks has been the more effective Houston back on a per-touch basis. Among 43 qualifying backs, he ranks 18th in explosive run rate and tenth-best in missed tackle rate. Marks is a viable flex this week with a good matchup. Indy has allowed the third-highest explosive run rate, the sixth-highest rushing success rate, the seventh-most yards before contact per attempt, and the fourth-highest missed tackle rate.

Rachaad White isn't a sexy name for Week 3, but he's a viable PPR flex option. White has operated as Washington's passing-down back with a 46.3% route share and 11.6% target share. He has averaged 11 touches and 58 total yards while accounting for three of the team's eight red zone rushing attempts. Last year, Seattle was eaten up by receiving backs, and this season they have allowed the 12th-most receiving fantasy points per game. White could have a nice week, as I expect Washington to be trailing for most of this game.

JK Dobbins left last week's game with what was reported as a hamstring issue, but then it was changed to cramps. Well, now he has been listed on the practice report with a hip issue, so who knows what is actually going on with him. Dobbins had a limited practice on Wednesday and full sessions for the rest of the week. Dobbins will be Denver's early down grinder this week. He left last week's game, so his usage is kinda muddied. In Week 1, he finished with eight rushing attempts and 36 rushing yards (zero targets). In Week 1, he played 40.4% of the snaps, had 53.3% of the team's rushing attempts, and a 15.2% route share. In his limited duty, he has posted a solid 13.3% explosive run rate and 2.39 yards after contact per attempt. Dobbins has a nice matchup on the ground this week. The Rams have allowed the fourth-highest rushing success rate, the sixth-most yards before contact per attempt, and have the lowest rate of contacting a back at or behind the line of scrimmage. If Dobbins doesn't score a touchdown, you'll likely be disappointed that you started him, though. He's a touchdown-dependent flex.

Jacory Croskey-Merritt got into the end zone in Week 1 and finished as the RB22 for the week. He wasn't so lucky in Week 2. Bill has been Washington's early down grinder, averaging 15 touches and 52 total yards. He has had a 41.8% snap rate, 43.8% of the rushing attempts, and a 21.3% route share (2.9% target share). Bill sadly has only two of the team's eight running back red zone rushing attempts. He has posted a solid 2.36 yards after contact per attempt, but struggled with only a 7.4% explosive run rate and 7% missed tackle rate. I don't expect Week 3 to be kind to him. Seattle has allowed the seventh-lowest explosive run rate, the fifth-fewest yards before contact per attempt, and the tenth-lowest missed tackle rate. Sit Bill this week.

Emmett Johnson is a viable flex option this week for deeper leagues. Johnson has been electric when on the field this season. He has averaged seven touches and 51.5 total yards while seeing one red zone rushing attempt. Johnson has posted 2.70 yards after contact per attempt and a 40% missed tackle rate with his limited workload. Those are fantastic numbers. Miami has allowed the 13th-highest rushing success rate, the 12th-most yards after contact per attempt, and the 11th-lowest stuff rate.

RJ Harvey missed last week's game with a hamstring injury. Harvey had a limited practice to open the week and followed it up with full sessions. He doesn't carry any injury designation into this week's game. I expect him to reprise the passing-down role he held in Week 1, especially with Jonah Coleman out. In Week 1, Harvey finished with seven touches and 41 total yards. He had a 53.2% snap rate, 20% of the rushing attempts, a 42.4% route share, and a 14.3% target share. Sit Harvey this week. The Rams have held backs to the sixth-fewest yards per target despite facing the fourth-most running back targets.

MarShawn Lloyd has seen discouraging usage to begin the season, averaging only 10.5 touches and 31.5 total yards per game. Last week, he played only 28% of the snaps with 33.3% of the rushing attempts and a 21.9% route share (6.9% target share). Chris Brooks out-snapped him with a 44% snap share while logging a 34.4% route share. Kaleb Johnson out-carried him with a 44.4% rushing attempt share. The Green Bay backfield has quickly become a three-way committee. We'll see if Lloyd can break out of it, but it's not looking good. This isn't how I projected this backfield to shake out after two games. Lloyd has managed a 21% missed tackle rate, but he also has only 1.63 yards after contact per attempt. He hasn't given the Packers a reason to increase his role to this point. This isn't the matchup that's set up for Lloyd to show out either. Atlanta has allowed the second-lowest explosive run rate, the second-lowest rushing success rate, and the seventh-lowest missed tackle rate. Sit Lloyd this week.

Tyler Allgeier has been the lead back for Arizona through two games while averaging 13 touches and 45.5 total yards as the RB41 in fantasy points per game. Allgeier has had a 59.7% snap rate with 43.1% of the rushing attempts, a 45.7% route share, and a 6.2% target share. He's had a solid 2.36 yards after contact per attempt, but a pitiful 9% missed tackle rate and 40.9% rushing success rate. Allgeier is a low-end flex play with a bad matchup this week. The 49ers have held teams to the fifth-lowest explosive run rate, the seventh-fewest yards after contact per attempt, and the sixth-lowest missed tackle rate.

Alvin Kamara logged his first game of the 2026 season last week and further muddied the New Orleans backfield with 14 touches and only 22 total yards. Kamara handled the only running back red zone rushing attempt. He played only 29.7% of the snaps but he led the backfield with a 33.3% rushing share and 17.6% target share while seeing a 23.1% route share. He was woefully inefficient with 1.89 yards after contact per attempt, zero explosive runs, and an 11% missed tackle rate. I don't know what Kellen Moore is doing with this backfield right now. I don't expect Kamara to see this type of usage on a weekly basis, but we have to see how this plays out. Don't flex Kamara this week as his usage could decline and it's a bad matchup. The Raiders have allowed the tenth-lowest explosive run rate, the seventh-lowest rushing success rate, and the fourth-lowest missed tackle rate.

Chris Rodriguez has been only a part-time player for the Jags. He has split the red zone rushing role with Bhayshul Tuten, with each back getting two totes inside the 20-yard line, but outside of his touchdown equity has been unplayable in fantasy. He has averaged six carries and 18 rushing yards per game with zero passing game usage (zero targets). This isn't the matchup to consider a touchdown-or-bust flex option like Rodriguez for Week 3. New England has allowed the 14th-lowest explosive run rate, the tenth-lowest rushing success rate, and has ranked 15th in missed tackle rate.

With all of the injuries last week to the Denver backfield, Jonah Coleman got into the mix. Well, this week he was reported to have picked up an ankle injury. He opened the week with a DNP. I'll update his status on Friday.

Atlanta's quarterback play has absolutely crushed Drake London to begin this season as the WR55 in fantasy points per game. London has an 18.5% target share, 1.78 YPRR, zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a team-leading 20% first-read share. London hasn't been bad, as he ranks 25th in separation score among 101 qualifying receivers after two weeks, but he can't throw accurate passes to himself. We'll see if he can get on track this week against a secondary that has held perimeter wide receivers to the sixth-fewest yards per target, but has allowed the 13th-most fantasy points per opportunity to the position. London should see a bump in volume with Penix back.

Davante Adams proved last week with his monster game that he still has plenty of gas left in the tank. I'll update his outlook on Friday. Puka Nacua's status will have a seismic impact on Adams outlook and usage and we need more info regarding Nacua's health before figuring out Adams' usage.

Jaylen Waddle PROVED in Week 2 that he is THAT DUDE and that I'm not insane for my offseason love of him. Last week, he finished as the WR9 in weekly scoring. Waddle had a 32.3% target share, 6.27 YPRR, one red zone target, three deep targets, and a 38.1% first-read share. I expect Waddle to continue to see similar usage weekly to this. The Rams have allowed the 13th-most fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers while ranking 15th in yards per target.

Last week, in the second half of the game, Mike Evans sustained a hip injury. He didn't return to the game. This week, he didn't practice until Friday, and he only had a limited session. He has been listed as questionable. I doubt that Evans will see a true full-time snap share in Week 3, but he could be limited and still log a 60-70% route share this week. In Week 1, he had a 63.9% route share with a 20.6% target share, 2.13 YPRR, two red zone targets, one deep target, and a 24% first-read share. In the first half of last week's game, Evans had a 90% route share, but he only had ten routes, so I'm taking much away from his lack of usage. I think Week 1 is a clearer picture of what we should expect his role to be weekly when healthy(ish). Evans could spit out WR2 production this week despite the limited nature of his deployment. Arizona has allowed the ninth-most yards per target and the 13th-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Tetairoa McMillan is the WR21 in fantasy points per game, commanding a 23% target share with 2.38 YPRR, a 27.3% first-read share, three red zone targets, and five deep targets. This week, he'll face a Browns pass defense that has the highest single high rate in the NFL (78.1%). Against single high, McMillan has a 20% target per route run rate (second on the team) with 1.40 YPRR, but last week he was the leading receiver for Young against single high with a 27% target per route run rate and 2.18 YPRR. I think McMillan will be the go-to for Young again this week. McMillan should have another strong week against a pass defense that has allowed the tenth-most yards per target and the seventh-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Through two games, Ladd McConkey has been underwhelming. Yes, his rib injury is part of the entire equation, but the entire Chargers offense has been a rollercoaster so far. Last week, despite having a 45.2% snap share, he had a 67.7% route share. Are either of these usage rates great? No. Also, when you pair it with the fact that in Week 2 he had an 11.1% target share and 11.8% first-read share, it's tough to feel good about McConkey right now. Overall, he has an 18.5% target share, 3.08 YPRR, an 18.4% first-read share, two red zone targets, and zero deep targets. In weekly fantasy scoring, he has finished as the WR12 and WR59 so far this season. He has a solid matchup this week, so we'll see if McConkey can bounce back, but he's just a risky flex play this week. Buffalo has allowed the sixth-most yards per target and the eighth-most fantasy points per target to slot receivers.

Malik Nabers dislocated his shoulder in last week's game. After opening the week with a limited practice, he followed it up with two full practices and doesn't carry an injury designation into this week's game. I highly doubt he's 100%, but at least there's no doubt in his availability this week. Nabers has a 75% route share, a 63.4% snap share, a 21.3% target share (25% TPRR), 1.37 YPRR, two red zone targets, two deep targets, and a 24.5% first-read share. I expect Nabers to be Jameis Winston's go-to this week. Nabers and Isaiah Likely. The Titans have allowed the fifth-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 15th in fantasy points per opportunity given up to the position. Nabers should have a solid stat line this week if Winston can feed him catchable targets, which, after last week's performance, is a BIG IF.

Rashee Rice's fantasy value is hanging on by a delicate string. Through two games, he is the WR29 in fantasy points per game, but without a score in Week 1, he would be struggling, and the fantasy community would be collectively freaking out. Rice's stranglehold on targets in the Kansas City offense has evaporated. He has a 9.5% target share... yes, you read that correctly. Rice also has only 1.62 YPRR, a 13.7% first-read share, and two red zone targets. Rice has a nice matchup this week, but he's only a flex play with the concerning usage. Miami has allowed the 14th-most yards per target and the seventh-most fantasy points per target to slot receivers.

After two games, Matthew Golden is the WR22 in fantasy points per game. Golden has a 25.4% target share, 2.32 YPRR, three red zone targets, two deep targets, and a 28.6% first-read share. Golden has been awesome. This week, he gets a Falcons' pass defense that has the seventh-highest single-high rate in the NFL (64.6%). Against single-high, Golden has a strong 25% target-per-route run rate and 1.90 YPRR. He should have success again this week against a secondary that will be without AJ Terrell and has allowed the ninth-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 16th in fantasy points per target allowed to the position.

Jalen Coker has gotten off to a hot start this season as the WR6 in fantasy points per game. He opened the season as the WR1 in weekly scoring and followed it up with a WR18 showing last week. Coker leads the team with a 24.3% target share with 3.00 YPRR, five red zone targets, four deep targets, and a team-leading 29.5% first-read share. This week, he'll face a Browns pass defense that has the highest single high rate in the NFL (78.1%). Against single high, in Week 1, Coker had a 30% target-per-route run rate (led the team) with 5.10 YPRR. Last week, Young focused on McMillan, and against single high, Coker saw his target-per-route run rate slip to 19% with 1.33 YPRR. I expect McMillan to be the primary against single high again this week, but Coker can still have a fantastic game. Coker should post a sexy stat line against a pass defense that has allowed the tenth-most yards per target and the seventh-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers. Coker is still dealing with the ankle issue that popped up earlier this season. He was limited in practice on Wednesday and Friday. He didn't practice on Thursday. His status needs to be monitored all the way to kickoff this Sunday.

Josh Downs is the WR36 in fantasy points per game while finishing as the WR20 in weekly scoring last week. Downs has a 21% target share with 1.91 YPRR, two red zone targets, one deep target, and a 29.5% first-read share. Downs has been a full-time player (85.1% route share) despite running 78.9% of his routes from the slot. Downs has a tougher matchup on the inside this week, but he's still a volume-based flex play this week. Houston has allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers.

In Week 2, Deebo Samuel saw his route share increase to 80% despite having only a 59.2% snap share. Overall, he has had a 59% route share with a 19.6% target share, 2.19 YPRR, three red zone targets, a 20% first-read share, and zero deep targets. Samuel is the WR26 in fantasy points per game and a solid play this week. Arizona has allowed the 14th-most fantasy points per target and the 11th-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Emeka Egbuka has been underwhelming to this point as the WR33 in fantasy points per game. He has drawn only a 17.7% target share with 1.32 YPRR, two red zone targets, three deep targets, a 20% first-read share, and zero explosive plays. I don't know if Egbuka will have a bounce-back week against the Vikings, who have the seventh-highest two-high rate (63.6%). Against two-high, Egbuka's target-per-route run rate drops from 20% to 16%, but his yards-per-route run climbs from 1.20 to 1.58. That still isn't an amazing number. Egbuka could surprise this week, but it's risky. Minnesota has allowed production to perimeter wide receivers, though, giving up the sixth-most yards per target and the ninth-most fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Through two games, Jameson Williams has been a fantasy black hole as the WR59 in fantasy points per game. Williams has had a 15.6% target share, 1.00 YPRR, one red zone target, two deep targets, and a 22.9% first-read share. Not great, Bob. Not great at all. I don't foresee better production for Williams in Week 3. The Jets have had the fifth-highest two-high rate this season (66.2%). Against two-high, Williams has had only a 19% target-per-route run rate and 1.24 YPRR. The Jets' secondary has also surprised me so far, giving up the 14th-fewest fantasy points per target and the sixth-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers. Williams isn't set up for a strong game in Week 3.

Well, DK Metcalf had another predictable down game as Christian Gonzalez shadowed him. Gonzalez followed him on 86.4% of his routes, holding Metcalf to four receptions and 27 receiving yards in his coverage. Overall, Metcalf is the WR52 in fantasy points per game with a 23.5% target share, 0.79 YPRR, a 36.7% first-read share, one end zone target, and five deep targets. I expect him to see shadow coverage from DJ Turner this week. Turner has followed Xavier Hutchinson and Emeka Egbuka so far this season on 52-69% of their routes. He hasn't allowed a touchdown in his coverage, and neither receiver surpassed 60 receiving yards in his coverage. Last year, in their two matchups, Turner followed Metcalf on 78.1% and 90.3% of his routes. Metcalf didn't surpass 50 receiving yards in either game against Turner (zero scores). Sit Metcalf again this week.

Michael Wilson has been the WR2 for Arizona as the WR55 in fantasy points per game. He has a 20% target share, 1.12 YPRR, zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 27.3% first-read share. The Arizona offense is sagging outside of Trey McBride. Wilson is a sit this week. The 49ers have allowed the 11th-fewest yards per target and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

After two games, Devaughn Vele has been the WR15 in fantasy points per game. In the Saints pass happy offense, he has had a 17.8% target share with 1.49 YPRR, a 22.7% first-read share, two red zone targets, and two deep targets. The per-route metrics aren't amazing, but he's seeing a solid market share of the offense and high-cholesterol usage. Vele is a strong flex again this week against a pass defense that has allowed the second-most yards per target and ranked 16th in fantasy points per target against slot receivers.

In his first game as New England's de facto WR1, Doubs tied for the team lead in target share and first-read shares, respectively, with 18.2% and 23.1%. Doubs finished with 96 receiving yards (4.80 YPRR), zero red zone targets, and two deep targets as the WR22 for the week. Doubs remains a volume-based flex play. He has a neutral(ish) matchup this week. Jacksonville has allowed the 14th-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers through two games while ranking 15th in fantasy points per target allowed to the position.

Adonai Mitchell flashed some fantasy upside last week as the WR25 for the week. Through two games, Mitchell has had a 23.1% target share, 2.16 YPRR, and a 25% first-read share. Mitchell has had a predictable 15.7 aDOT while seeing four deep targets (26.6% of his target volume) and a red zone look. Mitchell has a nice matchup this week and offers serious flex upside. Detroit has utilized single-high with 55.4% of their defensive snaps (tenth-most). Against single-high, Mitchell has had a 33% target-per-route run rate and 2.93 YPRR. Also, the Lions have struggled to stop perimeter wide receivers, giving up the 13th-most yards per target and the 12th-most fantasy points per target to the position. Mitchell popped up on the injury report on Thursday with a finger issue, but he managed limited practices on Thursday and Friday. He has been listed as questionable. I'm expecting him to play this week.

Stefon Diggs has had a fast start to the season as the WR10 in fantasy points per game. Diggs has a 21.7% target share, 2.17 YPRR, four red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 24.4% first-read share. He should see solid volume this week, but I don't think he continues the hot streak. Seattle has utilized two high at the seventh-highest rate in the NFL (64.4%). Against two high, Diggs has had a 27% target-per-route run rate but only 1.14 YPRR. Seattle has also shut down slot receivers, allowing the third-fewest fantasy points per target and the second-fewest yards per target to the position. Sit Diggs, if possible.

Denzel Boston is the WR12 in fantasy points per game. Do I expect him to keep producing like this? No. Is he FAR more talented than people gave him credit for in the NFL Draft process? Yep. Boston is tied for the team lead with a 21.2% target share with 2.85 YPRR (16.1 aDOT), two red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 27% first-read share (tied for the team lead). Boston remains flex-viable this week. Carolina ranks 16th in yards per target against perimeter wide receivers while allowing the eighth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity.

After two games, Dontayvion Wicks is the WR18 in fantasy points per game. He has a 16.1% target share, 2.72 YPRR, two red zone targets, four deep targets, and a 23.1% first-read share. Last week, his route share dropped to 64.3% from 81.8% the previous week. Am I freaking out? No, but it's something to monitor. Wicks is a nice flex play again this week. Chicago has allowed the most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Terry McLaurin has had a slow start to the 2026 season as he has failed to surpass 50 receiving yards in either game. I don't expect this to be the week that he gets rolling. McLaurin has had an 18.8% target share, 0.93 YPRR, two red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 24.4% first-read share. Seattle has utilized two high at the seventh-highest rate in the NFL (64.4%). Against two high, McLaurin has had a 24% target-per-route-run rate, but he has produced only 1.12 YPRR. Even if the coverage structure leaned in McLaurin's favor, I wouldn't expect much from him against a secondary that has allowed the fourth-fewest yards per target and fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers this season. Sit McLaurin this week, if possible.

This isn't the type of start that anyone projected for Luther Burden as the WR48 in fantasy points per game. Through two games, he has a 66.3% route share, an 18.8% target share, a 31.3% first-read share (leads the team), 1.79 YPRR, two red zone targets, and zero deep targets. We'll see if he can turn things around in Week 3 against a Philly pass defense that is struggling to defend the slot, allowing the tenth-most yards per target and the fifth-most fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Rashod Bateman assumed a larger role in the Baltimore passing attack in Week 2 without Zay Flowers. Bateman finished as the WR8 for the week. Bateman had a 29% target share, 88 receiving yards (2.84 YPRR), one red zone target, two deep targets, and a 38.1% first-read share. It was wonderful usage for the talented Bateman. I'm approaching this week as if Zay Flowers will be out again. This will vault Bateman back into last week's workload in a wonderful matchup. Last week, Washington's offense fell apart in the second half with Marcus Mariota under center. Dallas's pass defense in Week 1 is probably a better litmus test for their perimeter corners when evaluating this matchup. In Week 1, Dallas was 17th in yards per target allowed to perimeter wide receivers while giving up the tenth-most receiving fantasy points.

Chris Godwin has been an afterthought in the Bucs' passing game. Godwin has only a 11.3% target share, 1.39 YPRR, a 15.6% first-read share, zero red zone targets, and zero deep targets. Godwin is the WR42 in fantasy points per game. I don't foresee a better week ahead for Godwin against the Vikings, who have the seventh-highest two-high rate (63.6%). Against two-high, Godwin has had only a 5% target-per-route-run rate and 0.19 YPRR. His production has come largely against single-high through two games. Sit Godwin this week. Minnesota has allowed the fifth-fewest yards per target and the sixth-fewest fantasy points per target to slot receivers.

Xavier Worthy has been the Chiefs' real WR2 behind Travis Kelce this season with a 17.6% target share, 0.61 YPRR, four red zone targets, a 25.5% first-read share, and two deep targets. He hasn't turned the usage into much production, as the WR39 in fantasy points per game, but it's possible he changes that this week. Worthy is a decent flex play again this week against a secondary that ranks 16th in yards per target allowed to perimeter wide receivers.

Carnell Tate has been a nonfactor in fantasy through two games. Cam Ward's play has been dreadful. Tate is the WR58 in fantasy points per game. Tate has a 21.2% target share, 1.27 YPRR, zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 30.3% first-read share. Maybe this is the Ward and Tate breakout game, but it's tough to have enough faith in that to plug him into a ton of lineups (outside of deep leagues). The Giants have allowed the fifth-most yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Khalil Shakir has been a supporting cog in the Buffalo offensive machine this season. He has had a 20% target share but only a 58.6% route share. He has posted 2.15 YPRR with three red zone targets, a 21.1% first-read share, and one deep target as the WR47 in fantasy points per game. Shakir is a deep league flex only. The Bolts have allowed the seventh-most yards per target to slot receivers while ranking 15th in passer rating when they have been targeted.

Jordan Addison has done nothing over the last two weeks as the WR110 in fantasy points per game. Addison only has a 15.9% target share, 0.47 YPRR, one red zone target, zero deep targets, and a 16.7% first-read share. I wouldn't be shocked if he has a solid game, but I'm not projecting a massive outing. The Bucs have allowed the 12th-most yards per target and the 13th-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers. Tampa Bay has the second-highest single-high rate (70.8%). Since 2024, against single-high, Addison has a 19% target-per-route-run rate and 1.65 YPRR. Those are passable marks, but nothing to cut backflips over.

KC Concepcion is the WR45 in fantasy points per game. He is tied with Denzel Boston for the team lead with a 21.2% target share with 1.58 YPRR (3.7 aDOT), two red zone targets, one deep target, and a 27% first-read share. Concepcion has run 71.1% of his routes from the slot as the Browns' underneath option and seen a 36.4% designed target rate. Concepcion will have to break a big play after the catch to pop, but he has the talent to do that. He's a viable flex this week. Carolina has allowed the 12th-most yards per target to slot receivers while sitting at 15th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed.

Through two games, Courtland Sutton has been a distant memory in the Denver passing attack as the WR67 in fantasy points per game. Sutton has a 12.9% target share with 0.96 YPRR, one red zone target, zero deep targets, and a 19% first-read share. He's a shaky flex play at best. The Rams are 15th in yards per target allowed to perimeter wide receivers while also giving up the tenth-most fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Do I put any stock in Tre Tucker's 119 receiving yard output in Week 2? Not really. 42 yards of that box score came on one play. Tucker has shown the ability over the last two seasons to pop off with a big game at times, only to flub it up after that. Overall, Tucker has an 18.6% target share, 3.04 YPRR, one red zone target, a 23.7% first-read share, and two deep targets. It's only two games into this season, with one big box score skewing his overall numbers. If we pop open the hood of his deeper analytics, it further illuminates that this is more likely smoke and mirrors. Among 76 qualifying receivers, he has the 12th-lowest separation score and sits at 44th in route win rate. Those aren't numbers to invest in for fantasy. The Saints have allowed the 14th-most yards per target and the sixth-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers, which puts Tucker on the flex radar for Week 3.

After two weeks, Quentin Johnston is the WR99 in fantasy points per game. Wow, that really is bad. This entire offense looks broken right now. I hope the Bolts can get the train on the tracks this season, but it's not crazy to be very concerned about what we've seen to this point. Johnston has an 18.5% target share, 0.49 YPRR, a 21.1% first-read share, zero red zone targets, and one deep target. Buffalo has allowed the 14th-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 18th in yards per target. Johnston is a desperation flex only. In most leagues and formats, you're sitting him this week.

It was great to see Rome Odunze's route share climb to 81% last week, even though his usage didn't improve. Odunze is the WR52 in fantasy points per game with a 10.9% target share, 1.73 YPRR, zero red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 9.4% first-read share. I don't know what Ben Johnson thinks he is doing, but he needs to get it together. The Bears offense fell on its face in Week 2. It doesn't have to be complicated. Run your offense through your most talented players. Sit Odunze this week with a tougher matchup and his questionable deployment. Philly ranks 15th in yards per target allowed to perimeter wide receivers while giving up the 11th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Malik Washington has barely been flex-viable despite seeing a large portion of the Miami passing attack through two games. Washington is the WR51 in fantasy points per game despite seeing a 26% target share with 1.68 YPRR, four deep targets, zero red zone targets, and a 23.3% first-read share. Sit Washington this week against a secondary that has allowed the fourth-fewest yards per target and the second-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to wide receivers.

Jakobi Meyers is the WR45 in fantasy points per game. Meyers has been an afterthought in the Jags' passing attack with only a 5.8% target share, 1.55 YPRR, one end zone target, and a 5.3% first-read share. This isn't the matchup to look to him for flex production. New England has allowed the 11th-fewest fantasy points per target and the ninth-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Well, Brian Thomas Jr. wasn't shadowed by Patrick Surtain last week, and he still had a quiet game. Over two weeks, Thomas Jr. looks very similar to the 2025 version that disappointed fantasy gamers. He's the WR58 in fantasy points per game. He has had a 19.2% target share with 2.35 YPRR, one deep target, zero red zone targets, and a 21.1% first-read share. Thomas Jr. will have another quiet game this week. Christian Gonzalez will shadow him. Through two games, Gonzalez has followed DK Metcalf and Jaxon Smith-Njigba on 65.4-86.4% of their routes. Smith-Njigba destroyed him, but Gonzalez held Metcalf to only four receptions and 27 scoreless receiving yards in Week 2. Sit Thomas Jr.

DJ MooreÂ was knocked out of last week's game with a shoulder injury. This week he had limited practices on Wednesday and Friday as he sat out on Thursday. He has been listed as questionable. If he's active, I expect him to be a full-time(ish) player. The Bills might limit his snaps by taking him off the field on run plays, but he should still have a solid route share. In Week 1, he was the WR9 in weekly scoring, leading the team with a 24.1% target share and 33.3% first-read share while posting 100 receiving yards and three deep targets (zero red zone/end zone targets). Moore should reclaim his role as the team's WR1 this week. The Bolts should facilitate a strong stat line this week even if he's not rocking an 80% route share. The Bolts have allowed the eighth-most yards per target and the fourth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Wan'Dale Robinson has had a horrible start to his 2026 season. This can be attributed to Cam Ward's struggles. Robinson has only a 13.5% target share (4.29 aDOT), 0.96 YPRR, zero red zone or deep targets, and a 15.2% first-read share. Robinson is a low aDOT option again in a struggling passing offense, and he doesn't have any high-leverage usage. Robinson is a sit this week until he shows something, and he's droppable depending on the options on your waiver wire.

Keenan Allen might have finally hit the Father Time wall in 2026. Allen has a 17.7% target share with 0.84 YPRR, one red zone target, a 22.7% first-read share, and zero deep targets. Allen is the WR76 in fantasy points per game. Allen has a solid matchup this week, but it's tough to trust him as anything more than a deep league flex play. Houston has allowed the third-most yards per target and the most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Marvin Harrison Jr. has not been a part of the Arizona offense. Oh, he's out there with an 85.7% route share, but he's only drawn a 4.6% target share and 4.5% first-read share. Harrison Jr. is clearing out space for other receivers in the Arizona passing offense. It's sad but true. Until his role changes, he's a weekly must-sit, and he's droppable at this point.

Makai Lemon remains a bench stash only. Through two games, he has only an 8.1% target share, 0.15 YPRR, zero red-zone deep targets, and a 10.3% first-read share. Maybe with Dallas Goedert out, Lemon will see a boost in usage, but with how little he has been involved to this point, there's no way I can feel good enough about recommending flexing him into a fantasy lineup.

After two games, Kalif Raymond leads Chicago with a 21.9% target share, and he ranks second with a 25% first-read share. I don't know how to explain what Ben Johnson and company are doing. It doesn't make any sense. I have always thought Raymond was an underrated player, but not someone that YOU RUN YOUR PASSING ATTACK THROUGH. Yes, I'm frustrated that one of the smartest offensive play callers in the NFL is teaching us to never assume rationale coaching. Raymond has two red zone targets, one deep target, and 2.38 YPRR. I'm not flexing Raymond this week in a tougher matchup. Philly ranks 15th in yards per target allowed to perimeter wide receivers while giving up the 11th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Ted Hurst is an interesting deep league flex this week. Yes, last week he had only a 55% route share, but he played 72.6% of the snaps, and Jalen McMillan (two routes) wasn't a factor. Hurst had a 20.6% target share, 32% target per route run rate, two red zone targets, and five deep targets (21.8 aDOT). Minnesota has the seventh-highest two-high rate (63.6%). Against two-high, Hurst leads the team with a 21% target per route run rate and 2.16 YPRR. Minnesota has allowed production to perimeter wide receivers, giving up the sixth-most yards per target and the ninth-most fantasy points per opportunity to the position. I won't be surprised if Hurst has a solid stat line.

Michael Pittman Jr. missed Week 2 with a foot injury. He had limited practices all week and has been listed as questionable for Week 3. I'm expecting him to be back this week. In Week 1, he had only a 7.3% target share, 1.61 YPRR, zero red zone and deep targets, and an 8.7% first-read share. On a gimpy foot, this isn't good enough usage to entice me to plug him into a fantasy lineup this week. We also have no clue if he'll be a full-time player this week or if he'll split routes with Germie Bernard. Sit Pittman.

I'm approaching this week as if Brock Bowers will be out. He had only limited practices on Wednesday and Thursday before missing Friday's practice. The coaching staff stated that his absence on Friday was planned. I'm attempting to read the tea leaves here, but if he hasn't practiced in full yet and was held out for the walkthrough on Friday, I'm looking at that situation as he's more likely to return next week. Our Are They Playing Tool gives Bowers a 47% of playing this week.

After his monster game last week, Dalton Schultz is the TE5 in fantasy points per game. Overall, Schultz has a 23.4% target share with 2.24 YPRR, zero red zone targets, one deep target, and a 22.2% first-read share. Schultz could destroy the Indy pass defense this week much like Travis Kelce did last week (nine receptions, 101 receiving yards). Indy has allowed the 13th-most yards per target and the 14th-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Last week, George Kittle saw his route share increase from 47.2% to 52%, and he exploded with an 18.2% target share, 80 receiving yards (6.15 YPRR), and a score as the TE7 for the week. Overall, Kittle has a 16.1% target share, a 30% target per route run rate, 3.07 YPRR, three red zone targets, a 20% first-read share, and one deep target. Kittle should continue to see his workload slowly ramp up. He's a TE1 again this week. Arizona has allowed the fifth-most yards per target and the seventh-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Isaiah Likely is the TE3 in fantasy points per game (mostly related to his monster Week 1 performance. Likely's usage in both games has been amazing, though. He has a 76.5% route share (85.3% in Week 2), a 27.9% target share, 2.13 YPRR, four red zone targets, and a 32.7% first-read share. The matchup metrics aren't really worth discussing for Week 3 for Likely. In Week 1, Tennessee faced a split tight end room with Kenyon Sadiq, Mason Taylor, and Jeremy Ruckert. Last week, Dallas Goedert got injured. If Likely gets this type of volume weekly moving forward, the matchup doesn't really matter most weeks anyway.

Juwan Johnson is the TE7 in fantasy points per game with at least 10.6 PPR points in each game this season. He has a 12.2% target share, 1.69 YPRR, four red zone targets, a deep target, and a 13.6% first-read share. I wish Johnson had a higher market share of the passing offense, but I don't hate the healthy high leverage usage. The Raiders are 15th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to tight ends. Las Vegas has only faced the middling tight end rooms of the Dolphins and Chargers, so take that with a grain of salt. The Raiders do deploy zone coverage at the sixth-highest rate (85.3%). Against zone, Johnson has only a 12% target per route run rate and 1.60 YPRR. Those aren't amazing numbers, so expecting more than low-end TE1 production this week is probably asking too much from Johnson.

Through two games, Mark Andrews has seen solid usage despite being the TE15 in fantasy points per game. This is related to his zero touchdowns and is not indicative of his play. Andrews has had a 67.6% route share, a 23.2% target share, 2.13 YPRR, one red zone target, and a 30% first-read share. Those are all solid, if not VERY strong, metrics. Andrews should finally get into the end zone this week in a wonderful matchup. Dallas has allowed the eighth-most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Harold Fannin has had a rocky start to the 2026 season with TE32 and TE14 weekly finishes in scoring. Fannin is the clear third option in the passing attack behind KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston. Fannin has a 17.3% target share with 1.56 YPRR (3.78 aDOT), zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 13.5% first-read share. It'll be tough for him to produce this season if all he's seeing is low aDOT targets and zero high-leverage usage. Sit Fannin this week against a pass defense that has limited tight ends to the seventh-fewest yards per target and the eighth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity.

After two weeks, Colston Loveland is the TE76 in fantasy points per game, tied with Durham Smythe and Will Kacmarek. I can't make this up. It's insane and coaching malpractice. Loveland has a 72.5% route share, a 6.3% target share, 0.05 YPRR, two red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 12.5% first-read share. I legit don't know what to do with Loveland this week.
